walkthroughs.body_html:
Coastal Environments — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Coastal Environments brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Coastal Environments.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between mitigation and adaptation to climate change?
options: Mitigation and adaptation mean the same thing — both are about stopping climate change.
Mitigation reduces the causes (cutting greenhouse gas emissions); adaptation reduces the impacts (e.g. building sea walls, drought-resistant crops, early warning systems).
Moment magnitude measures damage while Richter measures shaking.
Mitigation is done by HICs and adaptation is done by LICs.

mcqs.q: Why has the Richter scale been largely replaced by the moment magnitude scale?
options: Moment magnitude measures damage while Richter measures shaking.
Mitigation is done by HICs and adaptation is done by LICs.
The Richter scale is still the standard scale used by all seismologists.
Richter saturates above magnitude ~7 and was calibrated for local Californian quakes; moment magnitude (Mw) measures the total energy released and works for all sizes globally.

mcqs.q: Why is 'renewable' not the same as 'clean' energy?
options: Moment magnitude measures damage while Richter measures shaking.
All renewable energy sources are clean and have no environmental impact.

Renewable means the source replenishes naturally on human timescales; clean means low environmental/health impact. Hydropower is renewable but floods habitats; bioenergy is renewable but can drive deforestation.
Clean energy means it doesn't produce any smoke when burned.
